# Top 5 posts from r/TrueFilm day

## 1. From The Atlantic: The Film Students Who Can't Sit Through a Film

**Score:** 152
**Body:** Cinepals: If you don't care to engage with the Atlantic piece (not long; cut and pasted to spare you the pay wall) at least check out the headline! (A pal turned me onto this one). EL

Headline: The Film Students Who Can No Longer Sit Through Films

The attention-span crisis goes to the movies.

By Rose Horowitch

Everyone knows it’s hard to get college students to do the reading—remember books? But the attention-span crisis is not limited to the written word. Professors are now finding that they can’t even get film students—film students—to sit through movies. “I used to think, If homework is watching a movie, that is the best homework ever,” Craig Erpelding, a film professor at the University of Wisconsin at Madison, told me. “But students will not do it.”

I heard similar observations from 20 film-studies professors around the country. They told me that over the past decade, and particularly since the pandemic, students have struggled to pay attention to feature-length films. Malcolm Turvey, the founding director of Tufts University’s Film and Media Studies Program, officially bans electronics during film screenings. Enforcing the ban is another matter: About half the class ends up looking furtively at their phones.

A handful of professors told me they hadn’t noticed any change. Some students have always found old movies to be slow, Lynn Spigel, a professor of screen cultures at Northwestern University, told me. “But the ones who are really dedicated to learning film always were into it, and they still are.”

Most of the instructors I spoke with, however, feel that something is different now. And the problem is not limited to large introductory courses. Akira Mizuta Lippit, a cinema and media-studies professor at the University of Southern California—home to perhaps the top film program in the country—said that his students remind him of nicotine addicts going through withdrawal during screenings: The longer they go without checking their phone, the more they fidget. Eventually, they give in. He recently screened the 1974 Francis Ford Coppola classic The Conversation. At the outset, he told students that even if they ignored parts of the film, they needed to watch the famously essential and prophetic final scene. Even that request proved too much for some of the class. When the scene played, Lippit noticed that several students were staring at their phones, he told me. “You do have to just pay attention at the very end, and I just can’t get everybody to do that,” he said.

From the November 2024 issue: The elite college students who can’t read books

Many students are resisting the idea of in-person screenings altogether. Given the ease of streaming assignments from their dorm rooms, they see gathering in a campus theater as an imposition. Professors whose syllabi require in-person screenings outside of class time might see their enrollment drop, Meredith Ward, director of the Program in Film and Media Studies at Johns Hopkins University, told me. Accordingly, many professors now allow students to stream movies on their own time.

You can imagine how that turns out. At Indiana University, where Erpelding worked until 2024, professors could track whether students watched films on the campus’s internal streaming platform. Fewer than 50 percent would even start the movies, he said, and only about 20 percent made it to the end. (Recall that these are students who chose to take a film class.) Even when students stream the entire film, it’s not clear how closely they watch it. Some are surely folding laundry or scrolling Instagram, or both, while the movie plays.

The students I spoke with admitted to their own inattentiveness. They even felt bad about it. But that wasn’t enough to make them sit through the assigned movies. Mridula Natarajan, a freshman at the University of Texas at Austin, took a world-cinema class this past fall. “There were some movies that were extremely slow-paced, and ironically, that was the point of the movie,” she told me. “But I guess impatience made me skip through stuff or watch it on two-times speed.”

After watching movies distractedly—if they watch them at all—students unsurprisingly can’t answer basic questions about what they saw. In a multiple-choice question on a recent final exam, Jeff Smith, a film professor at UW Madison, asked what happens at the end of the Truffaut film Jules and Jim. More than half of the class picked one of the wrong options, saying that characters hide from the Nazis (the film takes place during World War I) or get drunk with Ernest Hemingway (who does not appear in the movie). Smith has administered similar exams for almost two decades; he had to grade his most recent exam on a curve to keep students’ marks within a normal range.

The professors I spoke with didn’t blame students for their shortcomings; they focused instead on how media diets have changed. From 1997 to 2014, screen time for children under age 2 doubled. And the screen in question, once a television, is now more likely to be a tablet or a smartphone. Students arriving in college today have no memory of a world before the infinite scroll. As teenagers, they spent nearly five hours a day on social media, with much of that time used for flicking from one short-form video to the next. An analysis of people’s attention while working on a computer found that they now switch between tabs or apps every 47 seconds, down from once every two and a half minutes in 2004. “I can imagine that if your body and your psychology are not trained for the duration of a feature-length film, it will just feel excruciatingly long,” USC’s Lippit said. (He also hypothesized that, because every movie is available on demand, students feel that they can always rewatch should they miss something—even if they rarely take advantage of that option.)

Kyle Stine, a film and media-studies professor at Johns Hopkins, usually begins his course with an icebreaker: What’s a movie you watched recently? In the past few years, some students have struggled to name any film. Kristen Warner, a performing- and media-arts professor at Cornell University, has noticed a similar trend. Some of her students arrive having seen only Disney movies. Erpelding, at UW Madison, said he tries to find a movie that everyone in his class has seen, to serve as a shared reference point they can talk about. Lately, that’s become impossible. Even students who are interested in going into filmmaking don’t necessarily love watching films. “The disconnect is that 10 years ago, people who wanted to go study film and media creation were cinephiles themselves,” Erpelding told me. “Nowadays, they’re people that consume the same thing everyone else consumes, which is social media.”

Of course, young people haven’t given up on movies altogether. But the feature films that they do watch now tend to be engineered to cater to their attentional deficit. In a recent appearance on The Joe Rogan Experience, Matt Damon, the star of many movies that college students may not have seen, said that Netflix has started encouraging filmmakers to put action sequences in the first five minutes of a film to get viewers hooked. And just because young people are streaming movies, it doesn’t mean they’re paying attention. When they sit down to watch, many are browsing social media on a second screen. Netflix has accordingly advised directors to have characters repeat the plot three or four times so that multitasking audiences can keep up with what’s happening, Damon said.

Some professors are treating wilting attention spans as a problem to be solved, not a reality to accept. Stine, at Johns Hopkins, is piloting a course on “slow cinema”—minimalist films with almost no narrative thrust—with the goal of helping students redevelop long modes of attention. Rick Warner, the director of film studies at the University of North Carolina, deliberately selects films with slow pacing and subtle details, such as Chantal Akerman’s Jeanne Dielman, 23 quai du Commerce, 1080 Bruxelles, a three-hour movie that mostly follows a woman doing chores in her apartment. “I try to teach films that put their habits of viewing under strain,” Warner told me. “I’m trying to sell them on the idea that a film watched properly can actually help them retrain their perception and can teach them how to concentrate again.” Once they get used to it, students enjoy the challenge, he said.

But other professors, perhaps concluding that resistance is futile, are adjusting to the media their students grew up on. Some show shorter films or have students watch movies over multiple sittings. Erpelding, who primarily teaches filmmaking courses, has moved from teaching traditional production methods to explaining how to maximize audience engagement. He now asks students to make three- or four-minute films, similar to the social-media edits they see online. After all, that seems to be the only type of video many young people want to watch.

By the way, the last scene of The Conversation has the paranoid Gene Hackman destroying his apartment in a desperate and futile search for listening devices. He eventually gives up, and mournfully plays the saxophone amid the wreckage. It’s a brilliant scene, and worth the wait. 

### Top 7 comments and their replies (up to depth 10)

1. As someone who's been a TA for first year film classes, I want to say that intro film classes are not full of students who want to learn about film. They're full of students who need to fill an elective and think that the class about movies will be easy. 

That said, I'm not suprised that there are issues with attention span. I'm a huge movie person and even I have been affected by way social media has fucked up our brains. I've had to literally take my phone and put it in a different room when I watch movies. 

And I'm fifty-two.

This is not only a "young people's" issue, it's just most clearly seen in them. 
2. I took a film studies class in 2001 and distinctly remember someone sitting behind me in a lecture, as Citizen Kane started, say, "oh god it's in black and white." I think you always have morons take film classes because they think it's an easy pass. Plenty of people still love old movies
  - >  Smith has administered similar exams for almost two decades; he had to grade his most recent exam on a curve to keep students’ marks within a normal range.

A lot of film classes were an easy pass, but they required you to watch and absorb the film. Now there is a problem where students can't even do that.
3. This is probably going to be very, very bad for the art of filmmaking.

I mean, look at what happened to books.  When people stopped reading, books didn't go away.  They got worse.  Artistry fell by the wayside to make room for flat writing that was easier to understand.  I don't even think it was a conscious choice to sell books to an audience that doesn't read.  I think it's that the ***authors*** don't read.

We're going to end up with the same thing in movies.  Filmmakers who don't care about film, who just want to be perceived as filmmakers.  We already have movies that are engineered to not actually be watched (Matt Damon's point above), but now we're going to get movies made by people who do not fundamentally understand what a movie even is, or why anyone would want to watch one.
  - trends in literacy have not destroyed literature and great works are still being produced. perhaps the more pressing issue is that trends in literacy have made it harder to make a living writing, even for great writers. i suspect filmmaking will follow the same trajectory.
4. I can say from my personal experience this is way too real. I decided to go back to school and pursue a different major and also plan on getting a masters in film. Within my film classes, there’s maybe 25-30 students. Out of them, maybe 10 are engaged and five are actually deeply interested. The rest will sit on their phones during screening, not speak up during analysis days, and pay 0 attention on power points. The essays posted on our board are also either just AI or the most basic comprehension of whatever we were watching. It’s nice that half the class at least pays attention or is actually interested, but half the class sits on their phones or draws on their tablets or reads comics. Yeah, these are all real examples I’ve seen. It really sucks man. 
5. I'm an adult returning film student (36) and I've definitely noticed this in my younger classmates. They're enrolled in a film program and yet they have zero attention span for a majority of the curriculum. When discussing films with them, it becomes obvious how many of them are there because they want to learn how to shoot sports or music videos or reality TV. All of those things are viable careers I guess, but it's been really hard to find other students to collaborate with on projects because we want to make such vastly different things. It makes me feel like I'm too old to be pursuing this career, like maybe the job I want doesn't exist anymore and I should just pledge fealty to our new AI overlords...?
  - I'd take it as job security, these kids aren't going to know how to do shit, if they even make it out. 
    - i was worried about job security in my brainy new field (i'm 35) until i got back in the classroom and saw how young people read, write, type, use computers, do homework, and behave generally

i am no longer worried about job security
6. This article is misleading with its use of "film students." I don't think someone studying filmmaking as a career is the same as someone taking an intro film class(what this article focuses on). It's not surprising to me that a freshman who picks film as an elective then half-assedly watches their assignments, film class is the archetypal do-nothing elective class, that behavior is expected.
The Matt Damon interview and this seem the most pertinent to future filmmaking:

"From 1997 to 2014, screen time for children under age 2 doubled. And the screen in question, once a television, is now more likely to be a tablet or a smartphone. Students arriving in college today have no memory of a world before the infinite scroll. As teenagers, they spent nearly five hours a day on social media, with much of that time used for flicking from one short-form video to the next. An analysis of people’s attention while working on a computer found that they now switch between tabs or apps every 47 seconds, down from once every two and a half minutes in 2004. “I can imagine that if your body and your psychology are not trained for the duration of a feature-length film, it will just feel excruciatingly long,” USC’s Lippit said."

Reminds me of this:
"At the current rate of accelerating perceptual shrinkage, Julien predicted that th adolescent generation of the year 2000 would have no attention span whatsoever, hence no capacity to absorb any message longer than a single cinematic flash frame in duration. Even one-line gags and slapstick comedy would be incomprehensible to them. If, for example, they were shown a classic pie-throwing scene from the early silent films, they wouldn’t be able to recall, when the pie hit the face, where it had come from."

## 2. Thoughts on The Straight Story?

**Score:** 33
**Body:** Question, What are your thoughts on The Straight Story?

I recently rewatched The Straight Story and I gotta say, I still love this film. This is perhaps the closest to a normal film David Lynch will ever make and I just love that his most normal film is literally title The Straight Story. The film is just so wholesome and the interactions in the film just feel real, very Ernest Hemingway. It is also very simple, about a story of a brother who uses his lawnmower to travel to visit his estranged brother.

Richard Farnsworth gives a great performance as Alvin Straight and In my opinion, he should've won the Oscar for Best Actor that year. Farnsworth just gives the right pathos to Alvin and you can feel that he has a lot of regret but wants to make right and flat out refuses to let age get the best of him in seeing his brother.

Overall, it is a great film and is in my top 3 for Best David Lynch Films

### Top 3 comments and their replies (up to depth 10)

1. Well Lynch is known for a dreamy and ambiguous films, but what is their worth if you can't compare them to wakeful state The Straight Story presents. It's a simple movie with no twists and it sticks with you with it's clear message. For me it's an integral part of Lynch's work, a full circle.
2. When I was a kid, every summer we'd pile into the minivan and drive eight hours across the entire state of Wisconsin to visit extended family. Across hundreds of cumulative hours of travel I learned to appreciate the rural Midwest. It's stereotypical to say that rural life is more serene than urban life, but it's hard not to find some legitimacy in this view when you're passing through sleepy towns in two minutes flat and zooming past massive fields where the most exciting thing is a cow munching on some grass. It's endearing and captivating, and The Straight Story reminds me of that more than any other movie. It was shot on location, following the real path Straight took and letting the sublime simplicity of rural Iowa speak for itself. It's hard to explain why a white gravel driveway and a mundane field of wheat should be so meaningful, but they are.

What helps this is the really curt script. There's a central conflict, but there's little drama. Richard Farnsworth and Harry Dean Stanton don't need to have this huge history elucidated in order to sell this story. We the audience can understand how the bond between brothers generally works, and we understand early on that Farnsworth is close to death. Lynch shows you that that's all you need so long as you're earnest, and The Straight Story is one of the most earnest movies I've ever seen. Everything, much like in life, is episodic and seemingly arbitrary but never lacks for meaning because the writing is so direct and we never doubt where Farnsworth stands in the midst of all this. He's just a guy who has very firm ideas about life and family and he's all too happy to share them with anyone who'll listen.

The Straight Story isn't Lynch's best movie, but it is one of my favorites. It reminds me of a simpler time in my life and of a simpler place, and the unpretentious, beautifully composed story is just endearing in its own way. Sometimes you won't be in the mood for a Lost Highway or Fire Walk With Me, and I'm glad Lynch has this weird little outlier in his filmography where things can be uncomplicated and unabashedly nice.
3. When I first saw the film, the line "The worst part of gettin' old is rememberin' when you was young" struck me as something that had authenticity about it, even though I was young enough then that I would have to take Alvin's word for it. 

Boy, do I feel it more now. 

I love that film. Just about perfect as screenwriting, cinematography, acting, music... definitely primo Lynch. Even if it's different from his others, no one else would have told this story just this way. I'm glad Mary Sweeney (later Mrs. Lynch #3, although I think they were already parents to Riley) brought him the beautiful screenplay she had co-written, and that he ultimately directed it himself.

## 3. The Master (2012) meaning

**Score:** 12
**Body:** I see it as a representation of adding meaning to the meaningless, purpose to the purposeless, use to the useless. This is representatives by the repeated instances of repetition of seemingly useless and random activities.

## 4. What Have You Been Watching? (Week of (August 23, 2026)

**Score:** 3
**Body:**  Please don't downvote opinions. Only downvote comments that don't contribute anything. Check out the [WHYBW archives](https://www.reddit.com/r/TrueFilm/wiki/index#wiki_what_have_you_been_watching.3F).

### Top 8 comments and their replies (up to depth 10)

1. My main watch this week was Nicholas Ray’s **Bigger Than Life**, which I was obliged to pick up on DVD thanks to the wonders of region coding. It still looked fantastic. I haven’t seen much mention of cinematographer Joe McDonald, but he and Ray do pretty incredible things with CinemaScope considering much of it plays out indoors (though there’s a back garden shot to die for).

You’ve got James Mason as lead, and also producing, so things are off to a solid start before Walter Matthau shows up, after which you know satisfaction is guaranteed. It’s high melodrama, like a Douglas Sirk number, but with a whole array of twists and kicks along the way. It feels longer than its 95 minutes, but in a good way

I understand it wasn’t well received at the time, and I think possibly that’s because Ray wasn’t playing it straight - it’s subversive, but subtle with it. A lot of it stands up today - the parent getting excited by Mason’s drug-fuelled rant about the educations system is an all too recognisable figure.

I read a comment somewhere a while back that it’s also a kind of embryonic version of *The Shining*, which I can see the logic of. It escalates a little erratically, perhaps, but it’s enjoyable throughout and juggles comedy and drama with great confidence. It’s taken me far too long to get to and I’m glad I did - we just need a UK equivalent to the Criterion release or, ideally, a 4K with a matching theatrical run, as I’m sure this looks astounding on a proper screen.

I also watched **El Televior** (1974), recently released by Radiance as a double bill with celebrated Spanish telecom horror *La Cabina*. The set is called *Two Boxes: Televised Terror in Franco’s Spain* and is an easy recommendation - one of the TV releases of the year, for sure. I know *La Cabina* very well from its legendary 80s TV airing, and tracking down a bootleg DVD was one of my earliest internet triumphs. *El Televisor* was new to me, but I enjoyed it just as much. The characters are thoroughly endearing and, like *Bigger Than Life*, it delivers a well-balanced mix of comedy, drama, and finally - well, best to watch it. You might well see what’s coming, but it’ll still have impact (and if you haven’t seen *La Cabina*, this set will be your new best friend).

Not my most prolific week but both new to me and both excellent and well worth owning and revisiting, so still a great week.
2. **Excalibur (1981, John Boorman)** — I’m struggling to explain why *Excalibur* works as well as it does. It’s certainly not because it has such a strong cast (it doesn’t), and it’s not because the writing is particularly good according to conventional standards. The great production design accounts for some of it, though even then, the weirdly tacky under-lighting of a lot of scenes does dull the impact a bit. And yet, I would be lying if I said I didn’t enjoy almost every minute of it; and I don’t even really consider it to be a guilty pleasure, I think it is legitimately very good. Maybe there’s just something about the mythic ideals on display here that makes it hard to not find their straight portrayals compelling, even when the execution is a bit awkward. Highly recommended. **8/10**

**Bram Stoker’s Dracula (1992, Francis Ford Coppola)** — Okay, I feel like talking about this movie requires an approach I don’t usually take. Ordinarily, I don’t like to criticize adaptations *purely* for not being like the books they’re based on; I mention changes only if I think they meaningfully affect the quality of the story (whether positively or negatively). However, Coppola did not title this movie *Dracula*. He titled it  *Bram Stoker’s Dracula*. If you’re going to explicitly claim in the title that your version of the story is the same as the original author’s version, I feel like you then take on the obligation to stay at least *vaguely* faithful to said original version, rather than bastardizing it even more than previous versions to the point that it’s practically an anti-adaptation.

**START OF SPOILERS**

This choice feels particularly uncomfortable in light of the fact that the main changes Coppola makes are all about degrading the two main female characters as much as possible. By adding a tragic-romance plot-line blatantly ripped off from Universal Horror’s 1931 *The Mummy*, Mina’s ability to feel sympathy for Dracula is reframed to no longer be any sign of virtue on her part, but something *forced* on her by a twist of fate that she had no way of predicting. Moreover, where Stoker’s Mina was arguably more rational and self-controlled than any of the men around her — being the only one able to both feel pity for the tragic side of Dracula *and* still recognize that he was an abomination who needed to be destroyed — Coppola’s Mina’s decisions seem to only ever be based on what man she wants to fuck most at any given time. As soon as she is awakened to the true connection between herself and Dracula, she completely loses any further ability to resist his influence for the rest of the story, only accepting what must be done after Dracula himself repents and gives her permission to. Meanwhile, Lucy Westenra is rewritten from an almost fairy-tale-like innocent who falls prey to demonic corruption into the whore who contrasts against Mina’s Madonna, with the not-so-subtle implication that Lucy’s vampiric transformation and subsequent killing were her being freed to be her true self and facing the consequences.

**END OF SPOILERS**

Either one of these factors would be irritating on their own, but taken together, they become almost unsettling. Whether intentionally or not, calling this “Bram Stoker’s” in the title comes off like a kind of pre-emptive deflection, like they’re trying to ward off criticism of the movie’s problematic tropes by asserting them to be part of Stoker’s original vision of the story. And I’m not saying that an adaptation that was faithful to Stoker’s vision wouldn’t also have been problematic in a number of ways, but it wouldn’t have been as bad as *this*. Viewed in this light, the title feels not just misleading, but borderline libellous.

Aside from these issues, *Bram Stoker’s Dracula* is a pretty okay movie. The story is messy and doesn’t entirely hold together, but the production design and effects hold up remarkably well, and Gary Oldman and Anthony Hopkins are standouts in an overall very strong cast (with Keanu unsurprisingly being the weakest link). Still, I feel a little bit too uncomfortable with the concept here to give it a positive rating, so I’m going to leave this as **Not sure how to rate**.

**Bambi (1942, David D. Hand et al.) — re-watch** — I already really liked *Bambi* the first time I watched it, but holy shit, it was so much better than I’d remembered on re-watch. I think what really jumped out at me this time was how remarkably well it blends different tones. You look at the opening, and you’d expect the movie to be a very sanitized, cutesy view of nature — and, granted, for the most part, it is. But then you get to the few moments of real danger and violence, and it’s amazing how shocking Disney manages to make them without ever feeling like they don’t belong in the same world as everything else. Upgrading this from “highly recommended” to “basically perfect”. **10/10**

**Inside Out (2015, Pete Docter) — re-watch** — I feel like I’m the only one who doesn’t really like this movie. Re-watching it, I’ve realized that almost all of my issues with it come down to my thinking that the core premise is fundamentally unworkable. Really, it’s almost more of an anti-premise, in that it doesn’t so much serve to set up a story or any character arcs as to render the concepts of “story” and “characters” essentially meaningless. No matter how cleverly the writers work to incorporate all the stock dramatic beats that they want in Riley’s life, the impact never lands because I know from the start that Riley isn’t a person in any meaningful sense, but only a child-shaped automaton whose every act is decided for her by the Emotions. It’s like trying to write a profound emotional drama about watching a kid try to keep a Tamagotchi alive.

If I were to treat this as a kids’ movie, I might not find this to be such a glaring problem. But *Inside Out*, probably more than any other movie Pixar has ever put out, feels like a movie that is designed almost entirely to appeal to the parents, with only some minor kids’-movie flavouring for marketing purposes. I could imagine a compelling argument that it’s the best adult-targeted drama that could be made out of its premise, but that’s not saying much. **6/10**

**Skyfall (2012, Sam Mendes) — re-watch** — My opinion on this remains basically unchanged from the first time I watched it. The only major thing I’d add to my last review is that I have no idea what the hell the writers are trying to do with M’s character here. Ostensibly, one of the central themes of the movie is exploring M’s failures in her duties as a surrogate-mother towards her agents… except nobody, in- or out-of-universe, had ever thought M was *supposed* to be like a mother towards her agents before this, so there’s really nothing there *to* examine. My rating remains at a **7/10**.

**How to Train Your Dragon 2 (2014, Dean DeBlois)** — As I’ve said before, I liked but didn’t exactly love the original *How to Train Your Dragon*, so I wasn’t as disappointed by the sequel as a lot of people seem to have been. That said, I do agree with what seems to be the consensus that *How to Train Your Dragon 2* is a noticeable step down from the first movie, even if it’s not exactly bad in its own right. The first one at least seemed to have more of a cohesive purpose, whereas *2* feels like it’s trying to do a lot more things at once and doesn’t manage to juggle them as well. The great animation continues to be the main strength and is what mostly carries it into being at least decent. I’d say that the first is probably a 7/10, and rate the second slightly lower at a **6/10**.

**Movie of the week:** *Bambi*
3. **Doctor Who (1996, dir. Geoffrey Sax)**

As a Doctor Who fan, this hurt, but I was expecting that. The two legacy characters are characterized in ridiculous ways that flanderize one and turn the other into some sort of pre-Albert Wesker, post-Terminator nightmare. It does a piss-poor job explaining the premise of Doctor Who, which is problematic because this was supposed to be a pilot for an American revival of the original show. What I wasn't really expecting from this movie was how broken it was as an actual film. It can't settle on a tone, the pacing is really rough, and some of the creative choices are really baffling. The plot makes no sense and a pervasive sense of weirdness keeps you guessing for the entire runtime. The film has a sort of corrosive effect where any part of your brain geared to search for logic melts away as things just keep happening, and by the end when Eric Roberts is turning into some world-consuming god and Paul McGann is wearing a silly Clockwork Orange thing, the film becomes thoroughly entertaining. Mind you, it never becomes good, but after suffering through the Chris Chibnall era something like this isn't worth getting upset over.

**Planet of the Apes (2001, dir. Tim Burton)**

The humans talk in this film, which is a small detail but a massive flaw. There's not really a clear or logical reason why apes enslave and dehumanize humans in this movie, which really lances any of the existentialism of the original. It also means the protagonist isn't special anymore. Apes had a reason in the original film to be interested in and threatened by Charlton Heston, but here Mark Wahlberg is just yet another human. Sure, he's wearing weird clothing, but he doesn't demonstrate special knowledge or skills. He just escapes and likes freedom, like any human would in this scenario. The film wants us to believe he's friends with all these wonderful apes and humans, but unique relationships aren't well-established. Perhaps they should have thought about characterization before putting Wahlberg in the worst love triangle you've ever seen. Taking into account the film's setting of a wholly alien world where human society is untouched by hubris or ape uprisings, and here you have the dumbest possible interpretation of the original film. All of the fascinating themes and ideas of the original film are gone, and what we have left is a boring, generic, heartless blockbuster with none of the director's skill or charm. The ending is thoroughly fascinating, even if it is the stupidest thing in the movie.

**Godzilla: Final Wars (2004, dir. Ryuhei Kitamura)**

Godzilla: Final Wars was the culmination of fifty years of Toho kaiju mayhem, and oh boy is that fact inescapable. Final Wars is definitionally all killer no filler. You come to a kaiju movie for fun, wacky nonsense and Final Wars delivers in spades. There might not be as much Godzilla as in other films, but Kitamura makes up for it with fan service of the highest order: Xiliens, the obligatory American lead, the Gotengo, UN drama, Gigan, Ebirah, Anguirus, Roland Emmerich's Godzilla getting his ass kicked, a dedicated Minilla subplot, and so much more, all wrapped in the detritus of The Matrix with a hint of X-Men. It's one of those movies that feels like the best movie of all time while you're watching it. The action is entertaining, the filmmaking is strong, and the love for Toho and its legacy is endearing and infectious.

**A Modern Monte Cristo (1917, dir. Eugene Moore)**

I have no frame of reference for The Count of Monte Cristo, but I liked the character writing in this film. I like how sympathetic the protagonist is but how eager he is to manipulate someone he supposedly loves in the name of revenge. Considering its length compared to the source material, and considering how middling most other adaptations from this time are, I'm inclined to believe that this film flattens the source material, but I thought it was mostly decent in its execution regarding the central character arc.

**A Shot in the Dark (1964, dir. Blake Edwards)**

While I was watching this film, I was reminded of Airplane!, and how its screenplay was closely modeled after a 1950s melodrama called Zero Hour!. As it turns out, I wasn't too far off the mark. Edwards was set to adapt a serious play, but decided to retool it for his recently-established Inspector Clouseau character. This was a smart choice. The plot of A Shot in the Dark isn't very good, but Edwards and Peter Sellers never miss a chance to lampoon it. A lousy mystery deserves only a lousy detective. This is a marked improvement over The Pink Panther and is generally very entertaining. Sellers cannot miss a beat.

**The Buddy Holly Story** (1978) \*\*\* Gary Busey is memorable in this standard biopic that feels like a TV movie with an ending forced upon it, but rock and roll biopics were still a new thing at the time and it must have been more engaging than it seems today. **Big Wednesday** (1978) \*\*\* John Milius' attempt at *American Graffiti*, but where audiences could identify with cruising and hot rods and drive-in diners, it's harder to relate to the thrill of surfing. **Overheard** (2009) - Made by the same guy who did Infernal Affairs, and it's got all the over the top emotion of that movie. If anything, it goes harder and darker. It's obviously a morality play, and I'm enough of a fan of Johnnie To to be aware of the effect the Chinese government has had on the way crime is and law enforcement is portrayed in their films, but I love early silent films, and so many of those are just over the top morality plays, so I'm always going to be drawn to something like this. *4 stars*  
**Grandma's Boy** (1920) - Probably one of Lloyd's more famous movies. It's very, very fun. The story set up is actually quite nice, and I think the love story is really cute. This might be Lloyd's best performance. *4 stars*

## 5. Thoughts on Julien Duvivier?

**Score:** 2
**Body:** I've watched a few of his films over the years but seeing *La fête à Henriette* on the current Criterion Channel retrospective made think about just what a solid cinematic craftsman was.

Even though a young Francois Truffaut praised his work in the pages of *Cahiers* and *Arts*, I think Duvivier is kind of retroactively placed into the boring old *cinéma de papa* of pre-nouvelle vague French cinema. 

I don't think that's fair. For one, he wasn't just a director for hire. He consistently had a hand in writing his movies and sometimes actually was the sole screenwriter. Filmmakers of the caliber of Orson Welles, Ingmar Bergman and Jean Renoir praised him as a stylist. 

And his filmography has at least a few moments of narrative/thematic audacity that bely his reputation for safe, commercial cinema. I think of *Panique* (1946), a film about the mob mentality and scapegoating a social outsider made in the immediate aftermath of Vichy. *La fête à Henriette* is almost a 50s French precursor to something like *Adaptation.* or *Stranger Than Fiction*: a metafictional comedy about screenwriters making creative decisions that alter the film within a film.

All this to say that the Duvivier Criterion retrospective is definitely worth a look.
